"executive_summary": "This study uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with an analytical reference model to investigate how ions are distributed within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets. The authors simulate Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from 100 to 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. Their central finding is that in supercooled droplets, a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water forms and expels Na+ ions to a denser, more disordered subsurface region. This contrasts sharply with room-temperature behavior, where the ion distribution is nearly uniform. The authors introduce a reference analytical model that treats the droplet as a charged dielectric sphere and predicts an electrostatic confinement effect, where the ion experiences a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. This model agrees with simulations at room temperature but not at supercooling, where the heterogeneous solvent structure dominates. The work is motivated by applications in atmospheric and man-made aerosols, spray-based ionization methods in native mass spectrometry, and the use of droplets as micro-reactors for chemical synthesis. The authors anticipate that their findings will serve as a starting point for understanding supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecular conformations. The study highlights the importance of solvent structure in determining ion location and chemical reactivity, and it identifies gaps in the understanding of supercooled systems, which are notoriously challenging to equilibrate. The authors note that their results are consistent with previous computational studies for clusters at room or elevated temperatures, while extending the understanding to supercooled conditions. summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek, Ivan Saika-Voivod, Styliani Consta
summary.field_subfield: Physical chemistry / molecular simulation of aqueous nanodroplets
summary.executive_summary: This study uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with an analytical reference model to investigate how ions are distributed within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets. The authors simulate Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from 100 to 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. Their central finding is that in supercooled droplets, a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water forms and expels Na+ ions to a denser, more disordered subsurface region. This contrasts sharply with room-temperature behavior, where the ion distribution is nearly uniform. The authors introduce a reference analytical model that treats the droplet as a charged dielectric sphere and predicts an electrostatic confinement effect, where the ion experiences a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. This model agrees with simulations at room temperature but not at supercooling, where the heterogeneous solvent structure dominates. The work is motivated by applications in atmospheric and man-made aerosols, spray-based ionization methods in native mass spectrometry, and the use of droplets as micro-reactors for chemical synthesis. The authors anticipate that their findings will serve as a starting point for understanding supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecular conformations. The study highlights the importance of solvent structure in determining ion location and chemical reactivity, and it identifies gaps in the understanding of supercooled systems, which are notoriously challenging to equilibrate. The authors note that their results are consistent with previous computational studies for clusters at room or elevated temperatures, while extending the understanding to supercooled conditions. The study also discusses the implications for ion mobility-mass spectrometry data interpretation and the physics of jets, and it identifies future directions for research on the structure of low-temperature droplets containing unstructured peptides and complexes of ions.

Executive Summary
This study uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with an analytical reference model to investigate how ions are distributed within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets. The authors simulate Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from 100 to 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. Their central finding is that in supercooled droplets, a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water forms and expels Na+ ions to a denser, more disordered subsurface region. This contrasts sharply with room-temperature behavior, where the ion distribution is nearly uniform. The authors introduce a reference analytical model that treats the droplet as a charged dielectric sphere and predicts an electrostatic confinement effect, where the ion experiences a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. This model agrees with simulations at room temperature but not at supercooling, where the heterogeneous solvent structure dominates. The work is motivated by applications in atmospheric and man-made aerosols, spray-based ionization methods in native mass spectrometry, and the use of droplets as micro-reactors for chemical synthesis. The authors anticipate that their findings will serve as a starting point for understanding supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecular conformations. The study highlights the importance of solvent structure in determining ion location and chemical reactivity, and it identifies gaps in the understanding of supercooled systems, which are notoriously challenging to equilibrate. The authors note that their results are consistent with previous computational studies for clusters at room or elevated temperatures, while extending the understanding to supercooled conditions. The study also discusses the implications for ion mobility-mass spectrometry data interpretation and the physics of jets, and it identifies future directions for research on the structure of low-temperature droplets containing unstructured peptides and complexes of ions.

Research Context
Ion distribution in droplets is key to aerosol reactivity. Supercooled clusters have fascinated scientists for decades. Most computational studies focus on room or elevated temperatures. Supercooled clusters are challenging to equilibrate. Low-density cores emerge in supercooled water clusters. The distribution of multiple ions at supercooling is unknown.

Research Question And Hypothesis
How do ions distribute in supercooled nanodroplets? Does the low-density core differentiate ion distribution? Can an analytical model explain ion location? Is the effect electrostatic confinement? When is the effect more evident?

Methodological Details
Simulations used molecular dynamics in GROMACS. Water modeled with TIP4P/2005 potential. Na+ used OPLS-AA parameters. Temperatures were 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. System sizes ranged from 100 to 1100 molecules. Systems placed in periodic cubic boxes. Canonical ensemble with Nosé-Hoover thermostat. Thermostat time constant was 0.1 ps. Time step was 2 fs. Cutoff length was L/2. Cluster sizes from 100 to 1100 water molecules. Diameters ranged from 1.8 nm to 4.0 nm. Two simulations run for equilibration checks. Equilibration estimated from convergence. Tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) computed. Voronoi volumes used for density. Data for qT(r) and d5(r) from Ref. 31.

Procedures And Architectures
Energy is sum of electrostatic and surface. Harmonic potential centered at COM. Spring constant K(ε) defined. Maximum K at ε = 2.73. Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution used. Expectation value of r2 derived. EC more pronounced at low temperature. Rayleigh instability discussed. Simulation time 10-100 ns range. Diffusion coefficient ~10^-9 m2/s. Ion placed at surface for most runs. Ion placed at center for two runs. Conjugate-gradient energy minimization. Equilibration for N=776 after 400 ns. Relaxation time ratio τ1100/τ776 ≈ 2. Multiple ions start near COM. Cut off qT(r) at minimum at 1.6 nm. NPB equation for reference model. Surface charge density σ defined.

Key Results
Low-density core forms at supercooling. High density subsurface surrounds core. Na+ expelled to subsurface at low T. Room temperature distribution nearly uniform. Ion resides in highest density environment. Peak within 0.1 nm of subsurface peak. Surface layer ~0.3 nm thick. Multiple ions expelled from core. Two peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. Lower peak at 0.52 nm for one ion. Outer peak at ~1.5 nm. λPB ≈ 1.2 nm for 776 molecules. λPB ≈ 1.3 nm for 1100 molecules. λPB ≈ 0.8 with dielectric 75. EC evident for charge ±3e. Rayleigh limit defines stability. Model agrees with Voth et al. for N=100. N=100 does not form tetrahedral core. Na+ lies one or two layers in. Low tetrahedral structure near COM.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Heterogeneous solvent drives ion distribution. Dielectric constant increases with density. Surface does not provide good solvation. Layering affects small droplets. EC more pronounced at low temperature. Model extends to peptides and complexes. Implications for mass spectrometry. Relevance to atmospheric chemistry. Future study on conical deformation. Starting point for future research.

Contradictions And Limitations
Model fails at supercooling. Shape fluctuations affect decay. λPB interpreted qualitatively. N=100 lacks tetrahedral core. Small clusters have shape fluctuations. Noisy statistics for r < 0.2 nm. Sampling challenge in confined systems. Simulation time limits. Ion size effects not included. Hydrophobic effects not included.

Claims
Supercooled nanodroplets expel ions to the subsurface due to low-density core. Low-density core forms. Ions expelled to subsurface. Ion resides in high density. Peak near subsurface. Room temperature uniform. Model fails at supercooling. N=100 no core. Relevance to mass spectrometry. Future research starting point. Atmospheric chemistry relevance.
Electrostatic confinement explains ion location at room temperature. Harmonic potential at COM. Model agrees at room temperature. Spring constant maximum at 2.73. Model fails at supercooling. Shape fluctuations affect decay. Reference model for simulations. Extends to peptides. Conditions for EC identified.

Data And Code Availability
Data taken from Ref. 30 and 31. Details in SI. SI contains additional data. Figures S2 and S3 in SI.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two simulations for equilibration. Convergence after 400 ns. Relaxation time ratio. Multiple starting positions. Cut off qT(r) at minimum. Qualitative interpretation of λPB.

Ethical Considerations
No ethics reported.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 plots spring constant. Fig. 2 shows peptide distribution. Fig. 3 shows density profiles. Fig. 4 shows N=776 behavior. Fig. 5 shows multiple ions. Table 1 shows system sizes.

1. The core contribution. 2. The strongest evidence. 3. The future path.
